data.title: Daimler Truck ADR Earnings Call Signals Cash‑Powered Upside
data.description:
Daimler Truck Holding AG Sponsored ADR ((DTRUY)) has held its Q2 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.

Claim 55% Off TipRanks

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks

Daimler Truck’s latest earnings call struck a cautiously upbeat tone. Management highlighted solid revenue growth, surging orders and a major cash boost from the ARCHION deal, even as tariffs, rising costs and uneven regional demand pressured industrial margins. Executives framed Q3 as a transition quarter, with a stronger recovery and clearer earnings momentum expected into Q4 and beyond.

Group Revenue Growth and Profitability

Daimler Truck reported group revenue of EUR 12.3 billion in Q2, a 5% increase versus last year, underscoring resilient demand across key segments. Adjusted EBIT came in near EUR 800 million, while net profit reached EUR 1.5 billion, translating into earnings per share of EUR 1.91 and confirming solid underlying profitability despite headwinds.

Raised Full‑Year 2026 Guidance

Management lifted full‑year 2026 guidance, signaling confidence in the operational trajectory and demand outlook. The group now expects adjusted EBIT of EUR 3.6–4.1 billion, revenue of EUR 43–47 billion and a 7–9% adjusted return on sales, with industrial unit sales targeted at 340,000–370,000 vehicles and free cash flow of EUR 3.0–3.5 billion.

Trucks North America Turnaround

The North American trucks business showed a sharp improvement, with revenue around EUR 5.2 billion, up 2% year over year and unit sales rising 8%. Adjusted EBIT more than doubled quarter on quarter to EUR 435 million, lifting return on sales to 8.4%, while order intake above 35,000 units, up 156% year on year, and a 45% July Class 8 share point to a robust recovery.

Order Intake, Book‑to‑Bill and Backlog Strength

Across the group, demand indicators remained healthy, supporting visibility into the second half. Incoming orders were about 74,000 units, up 27% year over year, while unit sales reached roughly 87,000 units, an 8% increase, and a book‑to‑bill ratio of 86% combined with a backlog about 50% above last year, well above historical levels.

Industrial Cash Generation and Liquidity

Cash generation was a standout, with industrial free cash flow surging to approximately EUR 1.8 billion in Q2 compared with just EUR 20 million a year earlier. Net industrial liquidity climbed from EUR 7.1 billion to EUR 8.3 billion even after paying around EUR 1.5 billion in dividends and ongoing buybacks, and a second buyback tranche of up to EUR 1.1 billion is planned.

ARCHION Transaction Boost

The closing of the ARCHION transaction delivered a major financial boost, generating about EUR 1.4 billion in cash. After deconsolidation, net positive cash flow was roughly EUR 1.1 billion, with further proceeds of EUR 500–600 million expected as the stake is reduced, and the deal contributed a EUR 1.4 billion gain to reported EBIT from discontinued operations, with a net impact near EUR 953 million after impairments.

Zero‑Emission Leadership in Europe

Daimler Truck underscored its leading position in European zero‑emission trucks, albeit in a still nascent market. Zero‑emission truck sales reached around 1,400 units in Q2, up 21% year over year, giving the company about 38% share of the European heavy‑duty zero‑emission segment as ZET registrations rose to roughly 6% of total in Q2 from just 2% in the prior period.

Financial Services Performance

Daimler Truck Financial Services delivered improving profitability alongside a better credit backdrop. Adjusted EBIT in Q2 rose to EUR 58 million from EUR 23 million a year earlier, while adjusted return on equity climbed from 3.1% to 7.5%, supported by stronger interest margins and a healthier risk environment.

Strategic U.S. Greenfield Investment

The company announced a new U.S. manufacturing facility designed around modern and flexible production technologies. With start of production planned for late 2029, management expects the greenfield plant to provide attractive payback over time and materially increase U.S. capacity, supporting future growth and product rollouts.

Operational Improvements and Cost Discipline

Management highlighted ongoing efficiency efforts, particularly in Europe, as an offset to macro and cost pressures. The Cost Down Europe program and continued pricing actions helped Mercedes‑Benz Trucks deliver better volumes and profitability, showing that disciplined execution can partially blunt inflation and input cost headwinds.

Industrial EBIT Decline

Despite revenue growth, industrial profitability came under pressure, reflecting the tougher operating environment. Adjusted EBIT for the Industrial Business fell 22% year over year to EUR 780 million, with adjusted return on sales slipping to 6.8% from 9.2%, mainly due to tariff headwinds in North America that outweighed improvements at Mercedes‑Benz Trucks and Daimler Buses.

Tariff Headwinds and Ongoing Uncertainty

Tariff‑related costs weighed heavily on North American earnings, complicating the near‑term outlook. While a favorable U.S. content application offered some relief and helped underpin the guidance upgrade, management emphasized that tariff rules and potential retroactive accounting adjustments remain a source of uncertainty that investors must watch.

Negative Price/Cost and Rising Material Costs

Inflation and rising material costs squeezed margins at Mercedes‑Benz Trucks, leading to a negative net price/cost development in Q2. Management expects cost pressures to intensify in the second half and warned that Q3 profitability for Mercedes‑Benz Trucks will land in the lower half of the guidance range, highlighting the need for continued pricing and efficiency measures.

Halberstadt Parts Distribution Ramp‑Up

The ramp‑up of the new global parts distribution center in Halberstadt has been more disruptive than planned, affecting earnings in the quarter. Management guided that operational challenges will continue into Q3 before improvements materialize in Q4, making the facility a short‑term drag but a longer‑term logistics and service asset.

Daimler Buses Weakness and Outlook Cut

Daimler Buses faced a notably weaker environment, with unit sales and orders under pressure, particularly in Latin America and Mexico. Order intake was about 5,300 units, down 25% year over year, prompting management to lower the full‑year 2026 unit sales outlook to 20,000–25,000 vehicles, signaling a more cautious stance on that segment.

Portland Plant Closure and Restructuring

Restructuring added another layer of near‑term cost, as the company announced the closure of its Portland plant affecting around 370 employees. Management expects a high double‑digit million euro restructuring charge to hit second‑half results, especially Q3, positioning the move as a step toward a more efficient industrial footprint.

Zero‑Emission Market Size and Infrastructure Gap

Despite its leadership, Daimler Truck acknowledged that Europe’s zero‑emission heavy‑duty market remains small, with only 6% of registrations being ZETs in Q2. Executives pointed to charging infrastructure as the main bottleneck to reaching 2030 CO2 goals, which would require roughly 35% electrification versus the current low single‑digit share.

Regional Demand Variability

Demand trends varied significantly by region, adding complexity to the group’s outlook and mix. Major European markets such as Germany, France and the U.K. are tracking below average year to date, while Latin America’s overall market is down about 10% with Argentina particularly weak, weighing on volumes and profitability in those geographies.

R&D Capitalization Change and Earnings Impact

A change in R&D capitalization policy also pressured reported earnings, increasing the amount expensed through the profit and loss statement. The capitalization rate for R&D was cut to 10.7% from 17.7% in Q2 2025, lifting current‑period R&D costs and reminding investors that accounting changes can materially impact near‑term profitability metrics.

Forward‑Looking Guidance and Market Assumptions

Looking ahead, Daimler Truck’s upgraded guidance assumes a North American heavy‑duty market of 250,000–290,000 units and an EU30 market of 290,000–330,000 units. Trucks North America is expected to sell 160,000–180,000 units with a 9–11% full‑year return on sales, Mercedes‑Benz Trucks to post a 6–8% ROS, Daimler Buses 20,000–25,000 units and Financial Services a 6–8% return on equity, with Q3 shaped by tariffs, higher volumes and Portland closure costs.

Daimler Truck’s earnings call painted a picture of a company balancing strong demand, cash generation and strategic investments against tariffs, cost inflation and regional softness. While Q3 is set to absorb several execution and restructuring hits, management’s higher guidance and confidence in a sturdier Q4 trajectory suggest the medium‑term story remains constructive for investors tracking the stock.

data.description:
Galenica AG ((CH:GALE)) has held its Q2 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.

Galenica’s latest earnings call struck an upbeat tone, as management highlighted broad-based growth, expanding profitability and steady progress on integration and automation projects. Seasonal and transitional headwinds were acknowledged but framed as manageable, allowing the company to confidently reaffirm its full-year guidance and maintain a shareholder-friendly dividend policy.

Strong Top-Line Growth

Group sales climbed 7.1% in the first half of 2026 to CHF 2.136 billion, underscoring robust demand across Galenica’s portfolio. Even stripping out the 3.1% contribution from the Labor Team acquisition, organic growth of 4.0% outpaced the broader Swiss healthcare market.

EBIT and Adjusted Profitability Expansion

Adjusted EBIT increased 7.1% to just under CHF 118 million, and when excluding prior-year one-offs, underlying EBIT growth reached 12.6%. Profitability in the Products & Care segment improved from 9.3% to 9.6%, reflecting operating leverage and disciplined cost management despite a mixed consumer health backdrop.

Confirmation of Guidance and Dividend Policy

Management reaffirmed its 2026 outlook for consolidated net sales growth of 5.7% and EBIT growth between 6% and 8%, signaling confidence in the sustainability of H1 momentum. The company also reiterated its intention to keep the dividend at least at the prior-year level, underscoring a commitment to predictable shareholder returns.

Strong Retail and Pharmacy Momentum

The Swiss brick-and-mortar pharmacy market grew 5.4% in the first half, with prescription medicines up 6.9%, creating a favorable backdrop. Galenica’s local pharmacies outpaced the market with 6.2% growth, of which 4.3% was organic, while network expansion and the Puravita acquisition added roughly 1.9% to sales.

Healthcare Services and Patient Engagement Growth

Fee-paying healthcare consultations surged 27% year-on-year to 193,000 in the first six months, pointing to rising demand for pharmacy-based services. The Prescription Manager reached about 90,000 users, and with more than 1 million policyholders covered plus 25,000 vaccinations administered, Galenica is deepening its role in primary care.

Services, Homecare and Integration Wins

Sales in Services & Production rose 9.4% to CHF 63.4 million, driven mainly by homecare activities under the Bichsel, Lifestage and Medifilm brands. Management completed the merger of Bichsel HomeCare and Lifestage into a single offering, while Medifilm’s growing patient base and new machinery are boosting automation and scalability.

Operational Automation and Efficiency Progress

Automation at the Lausanne-Ecublens site has reached roughly 70%, improving capacity utilization and setting the stage for future cost savings. The Niederbipp distribution center is slated to switch to SAP by late summer, and Labor Team integration includes a new automated microbiology line in Goldach, all targeting efficiency gains from 2027 onward.

Lower-than-Expected Restructuring Charge

Extraordinary costs tied to winding down Bichsel’s pharmaceutical production came in at about CHF 30.4 million in the first half, below the initially projected CHF 35 million to CHF 40 million range. This lower burden provides some relief to earnings quality and reduces uncertainty around the restructuring program.

Product and Brands Sales Decline

The Product & Brands division posted a 9.8% sales decline in the first half of 2026, reflecting a weak cold and flu season that dampened demand for over-the-counter remedies. Reduced need for mosquito sprays due to dry weather and temporary stock corrections in international Perskindol inventories compounded the pressure on this unit.

Market Volume Weakness and OTC Pressures

Pharmaceutical volumes in Switzerland fell 0.6% overall, with OTC sales slightly negative at minus 0.3% and non-medication categories up just 0.6%. This subdued volume environment highlights the importance of service-based growth and suggests that traditional consumer health categories will remain vulnerable to seasonal swings.

One-Off Restructuring Costs and Transition Risks

The first half included one-off restructuring charges of around CHF 30.4 million related to Bichsel’s production exit, with minor additional costs expected in the second half of the year. The transition requires staff support and operational adjustments, introducing short-term risks but aimed at simplifying the group’s production footprint over time.

Working Capital, Cash Flow and Leverage Pressure

Cash flow was weaker than a year ago, as seasonal net working capital needs, delayed billing and ERP-related inventory buildup weighed on liquidity. Adjusted net debt rose to CHF 837 million, corresponding to leverage of about 2.7 times, above the targeted 2.2 to 2.3 times ratio that management plans to reach by year-end.

Wholesale Physician Segment Lagging Market

While wholesale sales advanced 4.3% overall, the physician customer segment underperformed a market that grew 3.1%, reflecting deliberate portfolio and channel decisions. Management pointed to actions such as closing a mail-order pharmacy as factors limiting nominal growth, even as resources are redirected to more attractive segments.

Regulatory and Market Risks

New regulatory measures include a CHF 5 cut in handling fees and a 10% price reduction on the top ten laboratory tests, squeezing revenue per transaction. Longer term, liberalization of mail-order OTC trade and changes to homecare remuneration add uncertainty, though management expects these shifts to materialize gradually and remain manageable.

Forward-Looking Guidance and Outlook

Galenica’s reiterated guidance for mid-single-digit sales growth and mid-to-high single-digit EBIT growth in 2026 rests on continued pharmacy expansion, service uptake and efficiency gains. With capex guided at CHF 80 million to CHF 90 million and leverage targeted lower by year-end, management is signaling a balance between investment, deleveraging and attractive shareholder returns.

Galenica’s earnings call painted a picture of a healthcare group successfully riding structural demand for pharmacy and homecare services while navigating seasonal and regulatory headwinds. For investors, the combination of solid top-line growth, rising underlying profitability, disciplined capital allocation and confirmed guidance supports a cautiously optimistic stance on the stock.

Executives underscored strong revenue gains, healthier returns on invested capital, and a younger fleet, while acknowledging pressures from higher depreciation, thinner Seminovos margins, and elevated capex as deliberate moves to support long-term value.

Consolidated Revenue Surges on All Business Lines

Localiza delivered consolidated net revenue of BRL 12.3 billion in the second quarter of 2026, a 24.5% jump versus the prior year. Management credited the performance to simultaneous growth in Rent a Car, Fleet Rental, and Seminovos, which together reinforced the company’s scale and diversification across its core segments.

Profitability Expands with Strong Bottom Line

Profitability moved higher alongside revenue, with EBIT reaching BRL 2.3 billion, up 15.1% year over year, and net income climbing 30.6% to BRL 1.0 billion. EBITDA grew 14.1% to BRL 3.8 billion, reflecting operational efficiencies and disciplined cost management even as the company continued investing in fleet renewal and retail expansion.

Car Rental Segment Gains Volume and Pricing Power

In the Car Rental segment, net revenue rose 11.2% year over year to BRL 2.8 billion, supported by a 6.8% increase in rental days and a 3.7% improvement in average daily rates. Utilization climbed 3.3 percentage points to 81.9%, pointing to better pricing discipline and productivity gains that help cushion the impact of higher fleet costs.

Fleet Rental Recovery Boosts Margins and Utilization

Fleet Rental revenue increased 5.8% to BRL 2.4 billion as Localiza benefited from higher average daily rates of 5.6% and utilization near full capacity at 96.7%. The segment’s EBITDA margin expanded by 4.6 percentage points to 75.6%, underscoring improved efficiency and the resilience of contract-based revenue streams even in a volatile macro environment.

Seminovos Sales Accelerate to Support Fleet Rotation

Seminovos operations accelerated sharply, with about 92,000 vehicles sold in the quarter versus roughly 68,000 a year earlier, pushing segment revenue to around BRL 7.1 to 7.2 billion, up about 38.9%. Management stressed that maintaining a sales pace of about 90,000 cars per quarter is crucial to optimizing fleet cycles and unlocking value from vehicle disposals.

Fleet Rejuvenation Cuts Costs and Lowers Average Age

The company continued rejuvenating its fleet, reducing the operating fleet’s average age by 24.1% year over year to 8.2 months from 10.8 months. The average age of cars sold also fell to 19.4 months from 22.2 months, which management expects will lower maintenance and preparation expenses and improve customer experience through newer vehicles.

Solid Cash Generation and Strengthened Liquidity

Localiza generated BRL 1.8 billion in free cash flow before interest in the first half of the year and ended the quarter with BRL 11.4 billion in cash, enough to cover short-term obligations. The company completed a roughly BRL 7 billion refinancing in July, extending debt maturities and lowering the average cost of funding, bolstering liquidity and financial flexibility.

Return Metrics Improve as Leverage Stays Under Control

Return on invested capital remained robust, with annualized ROIC for the first half at 16.1% and a 6.1 percentage point spread over the after-tax cost of debt, showing value creation even under higher rate conditions. Net debt to EBITDA stood at 2.16 times, while the net-to-fleet value ratio improved from 59% to 55%, signaling healthier balance sheet efficiency despite larger absolute debt.

Conservative Depreciation Approach in a Changing Market

Management continued to apply conservative depreciation assumptions in light of new automotive entrants and fresh model launches that may influence residual values. Annualized depreciation per vehicle climbed to BRL 8,243 in Rent a Car and BRL 9,198 in Fleet Rental and is expected to rise mildly, putting some pressure on operating expenses but reducing the risk of future write-downs.

Seminovos Margins Hit by Mix and Strategic Investments

Seminovos profitability lagged, with Brazil’s EBITDA margin at just 1.9% and 1.2 percentage points lower than in the first quarter of 2026, as the mix shifted more heavily toward SUVs with lower gross margins. Additional short-term drag came from rebranding stores, increasing headcount, and boosting marketing, which management framed as upfront investments to strengthen the retail channel and support higher-value sales.

High Net Car Capex Consumes Rental Cash Generation

During the first half, rental operations generated BRL 5.2 billion in cash, but net car capex of the same amount plus BRL 161 million in other investments fully absorbed that flow. Working capital actions, including a BRL 2.0 billion rise in payables, helped fund the investment cycle, yet left only modest free cash, highlighting the capital intensity of fleet expansion and renewal.

Net Debt Rises with Heavy Vehicle Purchases

Net debt increased to BRL 32.4 billion, 4.2% higher than at year-end 2025, reflecting purchases of 120,626 vehicles against 92,043 sales in the period. Management argued that leverage remains manageable, noting that fleet growth and a younger asset base support future earnings, but investors will likely watch absolute debt levels closely as capex remains high.

Macro and Industry Risks Keep Management on Guard

Executives acknowledged risks from new automaker entrants, possible pricing pressure in both new and used cars, and evolving tax reforms that could affect residual values and pricing dynamics. The company is monitoring these trends and maintaining cautious assumptions in its planning, aiming to shield its balance sheet from adverse changes in the broader automotive market.

Financing Headwinds for Used Car Buyers

Localiza noted a modest softening in external financing approvals for used car buyers, which could weigh on Seminovos demand if it worsens. However, management indicated that commercial efficiencies and operational levers have so far offset this headwind, allowing the company to sustain high sales volumes through improved processes and customer outreach.

Guidance Signals Continued Growth and Discipline

Looking ahead to the second half of 2026, Localiza plans to keep growing net revenue in Rent a Car and Fleet Rental, while sustaining Seminovos sales at roughly 90,000 vehicles per quarter and increasing the share of retail customers. The company aims to maintain its focus on cost and productivity gains, leverage technology, and preserve capital discipline even as depreciation trends slightly higher and the macro environment remains uncertain.

Localiza’s earnings call painted a picture of a company leaning into growth with a younger fleet, stronger margins, and solid returns, while shouldering higher capex and cautious depreciation. For investors, the key takeaway is that management is prioritizing long-term competitiveness and balance sheet health, even at the cost of near-term margin pressure in selected areas like Seminovos.

Strong Top-Line Growth

Revenue jumped 48% year over year to $777 million, underscoring a sharp rebound in demand for Lionsgate’s film and TV content. Management credited the surge largely to the Motion Picture division and ongoing monetization of the company’s deep content library, signaling that both new releases and catalog titles are pulling their weight.

Motion Picture Segment Outperformance

The Motion Picture segment was the star of the quarter, with revenue more than doubling to $587 million and segment profit hitting $105 million. That marks the highest first-quarter Motion Picture profit in the company’s history, giving Lionsgate fresh firepower and reinforcing the strategic value of its theatrical and franchise slate.

Improved Profitability Metrics

Adjusted OIBDA rose to $79 million, while Studio segment profit, which combines Motion Picture and Television before corporate costs, climbed to $115 million. Operating income reached $26 million, showcasing better cost control and operating leverage even as the company continues to invest heavily in content and growth initiatives.

Free Cash Flow and Deleveraging Progress

Free cash flow hit $129 million for the quarter, giving Lionsgate more flexibility to manage debt and invest in future projects. Net debt fell by $121 million to about $1.5 billion and leverage improved to 4.3 times, achieving the company’s mid‑4x target earlier than expected and easing balance sheet concerns.

Robust Backlog and Library Strength

Lionsgate’s film and television backlog climbed to $1.5 billion, up 21% from a year ago, providing strong revenue visibility for coming periods. The library generated $987 million over the trailing 12 months, roughly flat year over year, with evergreen titles like “Dirty Dancing” still meaningfully contributing to the bottom line.

Box Office and Franchise Momentum

Within four months, Lionsgate launched two branded titles, “Michael” and “The Housemaid,” pushing its domestic box office share above 10%. Early indicators for “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” are encouraging, and several other franchise films have wrapped production, laying the groundwork for future box office and downstream revenue.

Strategic TV Wins and Diversified Distribution

On the television side, the studio is close to achieving renewals on all 13 scripted series across 12 different buyers, reflecting broad demand from streamers and networks. Recent orders, including Amazon’s “DINKS” and the “Trauma” series for Prime Video U.K. and Paramount+ in the U.S., underscore a diversified buyer base that reduces reliance on any single platform.

High-Value Licensing Deals

Lionsgate struck a major licensing agreement for its “Power” franchise, placing the first four series on Netflix internationally and the original series worldwide for three years starting in November. Management described the deal as transformative, highlighting both the enduring appeal of the franchise and the appetite streamers have for proven library series.

Strong Liquidity Position

The company ended the quarter with $426 million of unrestricted cash and $800 million of available capacity on its revolving credit facility. With no major near-term corporate debt maturities, Lionsgate emphasized that its liquidity cushion is ample, giving it room to weather industry swings and pursue selective growth opportunities.

Operational and Strategic Initiatives

Management pointed to growing momentum at its 3 Arts business, which is expanding into areas like sports and creator-led content to broaden the revenue base. The company also reported about 95% employee adoption of AI tools, aiming to cut costs, speed up production workflows and unlock new monetization angles across the content lifecycle.

Reported GAAP Loss Per Share

Despite the operational momentum, Lionsgate posted a diluted GAAP loss per share of $0.10, reminding investors that the turnaround is still in progress. On an adjusted basis, diluted EPS came in at $0.06, showing improvement but underscoring that headline earnings remain constrained by non-cash and one-time items.

Television Revenue and Profit Timing

Television revenue fell to $189 million and segment profit to $10 million, both down from the prior year, largely because of timing in episodic deliveries. Management framed this softness as temporary, with expectations that TV results will improve later in the fiscal year as deliveries ramp and new seasons hit the schedule.

Library Revenue Essentially Flat

Trailing 12‑month library revenue held steady at $987 million, showing stability but not growth in this key profit driver. While management highlighted the durability of its catalog performance, the flat trend suggests incremental upside will depend more on new hits and superior deal-making than on organic library expansion alone.

Leverage Still Material

Even with leverage down to 4.3 times, the roughly $1.5 billion net debt load remains a significant factor in the investment story. Management also flagged that a potential 3 Arts transaction later in the year could temporarily push leverage up by around half a turn, keeping balance sheet discipline squarely in focus.

Earnings Dependent on Hit Content

Executives acknowledged that earnings still lean heavily on a small number of major titles, with three or four key releases capable of swinging results. This event-driven model creates volatility and execution risk, making the success of upcoming films and series central to whether Lionsgate can sustain its current momentum.

Industry and M&A Uncertainty

The company also flagged ongoing industry consolidation and uncertain transactions, including developments around major competitors, as a source of drag. Management argued that delays and ambiguity around deal-making are generally negative for the business, even though a stronger competitor base can ultimately boost demand for Lionsgate’s content.

Forward-Looking Guidance and Outlook

Looking ahead, management reaffirmed its fiscal 2027 outlook and projected significant growth in adjusted OIBDA and free cash flow this year and beyond. The company expects continued deleveraging toward 3–3.5 times by fiscal 2028 and below 3 times thereafter, with improving TV profits and the Q3 release of “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” cited as key drivers of the next leg of growth.

Lionsgate’s latest call painted the picture of a studio in resurgence, powered by a revitalized film slate, stable library earnings and better cash discipline. Investors will need to weigh the strong operational trajectory and healthier balance sheet against lingering GAAP losses, elevated leverage and dependence on a handful of big bets, but the near-term narrative has clearly shifted in the company’s favor.

MBIA Insurance Corp. saw its claims‑paying resources rise to $342 million, up $25 million, supporting management’s message that the group remains able to meet insured obligations.

Insured Gross Par at MBIA Insurance Corp. Declines

MBIA Insurance Corp.’s insured gross par fell to just under $1.8 billion as of June 30, 2026, representing a 12% decline from year‑end. The drop was driven by regular amortization in the legacy portfolio, continuing the long‑running strategy of shrinking risk exposure over time.

GAAP Losses Narrow but Remain Meaningful

MBIA reported a consolidated GAAP net loss of $46 million for Q2 2026, or negative $0.91 per share, compared with a $56 million loss a year ago. On an adjusted basis, the net loss improved slightly to $7 million, or negative $0.14 per share, reflecting modest progress but not yet a return to profitability.

Liquidity and Capital Actions Under Review

Holding company unencumbered cash and liquid assets totaled $337 million, down from $357 million at year‑end, but still substantial. Management noted there is $71 million of remaining share repurchase capacity and up to $35 million of custodial receipts that could be monetized if market pricing is attractive.

Year‑to‑Date Losses Pressure Equity

For the first six months of 2026, MBIA booked a consolidated net loss of $86 million, extending cumulative damage to shareholder equity. These losses continue to weigh heavily on book value, underscoring why the company’s shares trade more on option‑like outcomes than on traditional earnings metrics.

Book Value Deeply in Negative Territory

MBIA Inc.’s book value per share was a negative $45.58 as of June 30, 2026, deteriorating by $1.31 since year‑end. Within that, MBIA Insurance Corp. showed an even more negative book value of $54.26 per share, highlighting the depth of legacy stresses on the consolidated balance sheet.

PREPA Legal and Political Uncertainty Persists

The company stressed that PREPA remains a material unresolved exposure, with $390 million of gross par still outstanding and litigation ongoing. Uncertainty around court processes and the composition of the Puerto Rico Oversight Board continues to complicate settlement prospects and investor visibility.

Bondholders Reject Oversight Board Settlement Terms

The Oversight Board nearly doubled its proposed PREPA settlement to roughly $3 billion from $1.6 billion, but major bondholders rejected it. Management noted trading references around $0.75 on the dollar versus an offer near $0.30‑$0.40, illustrating the wide gap between market expectations and proposed recoveries.

Holding Company Cash Burn Moderates but Continues

Unencumbered cash and liquid assets at the holding company slipped by $20 million since year‑end to $337 million, mainly due to debt service and operating costs. Investment income partially offset the outflows, yet the gradual cash burn remains a key risk metric watched by equity and credit investors.

Non‑Recurring Gains Cushion Quarterly Losses

Management acknowledged that Q2 results benefited from one‑time items, including a reversal of legal expenses tied to Zohar CDO recoveries and foreign exchange gains. These non‑recurring factors helped limit the GAAP loss but do not signal sustainable improvement in the underlying business.

Leverage and Collateral Constraints Still Significant

Despite an improved leverage ratio, National’s 21:1 gross par to capital remains elevated versus most traditional insurers. The corporate segment also has about $183 million of assets pledged to guaranteed investment agreement holders, restricting flexibility in managing liquidity and capital.

Management emphasized that resolving PREPA is the company’s central strategic task, with remaining scheduled debt service of $20 million in both 2027 and 2028.
